You are playing ∑ Experimental · symbols first. Above the scene floats the real equation that holds right now — with values that change when you do something. It is a plane in the same 3D world: it tilts with the camera.

So that you can read the equation with your eyes, it has mnemonics. Every symbol is a picture (a glyph): the letter with a pictogram of what it does — try hovering over α. Three main rules: colour = WHO, size = HOW MUCH, spin = PHASE. All the rules and the glyph dictionary are under 🔑:
Before every task I will first show you its equation (the ∑ card) and only then the picture. Symbols in conversations have the same colours — α always blue, β always red.

Hi! Welcome to Hilbert Island. I am Spark — a little spark of light that will guide you around the island. (Don’t mix me up with the amplitude symbol — that one has a magnitude and a phase, I just glow.)

And you are Little Psi — the quantum state ψ. You are not a little ball with a position and a velocity. You are a rule for predictions: you tell what outcomes anyone who asks you something (measures you) will get.
See that golden hand turning around you? That is your global phase. It turns, but nobody in the world can measure it. Remember: the global phase is unobservable, the relative phase is not.

There are 8 portals around the island. Behind each one a mentor is waiting — Euler, Stern, Bloch, Feynman, Dirac, Rabi, Bell and Bohr. They will teach you the language, the symbols and the right pictures of the quantum world.
Above the island circles Ketvarr, the quantum dragon. Each mentor will teach you one Word of Power. Once you have all eight, climb Dragon’s Peak in the north and defeat him.
The goal is not to compute integrals. The goal is intuition: knowing what an amplitude is, what a probability is, what a measurement does and where classical analogies stop working.
Controls: WASD move, mouse drag camera, E enter/talk, C Codex of symbols, M map, H help. Start with portal 1!
You are playing the experimental symbols type, so the ring has an extra portal 0 — the Hall of Symbols. It teaches you to read the colours and shapes of the equations; I suggest starting there.
New to the quantum world? Switch the difficulty (top right) to 🫶 Layman — I will explain everything in everyday words.

One more thing: the island is full of classical misconceptions. Fight them with spells 1–7 (Tab = target, right-click = attack), gather experience and money, shop at Planck’s by the fountain (B = bags). Talk to me again and I will give you your first quest.
. Don’t forget: amplitudes interfere, probabilities are only measured.
The meadows beyond the portals are crawling with Hidden Variables. They whisper that the outcome was fixed in advance.
Bell proved that no local hidden variables can explain quantum correlations. Debunk 5 of them — and come back to me.
Well done. Remember: quantum probabilities are not just our ignorance.
Billiard-Ball Electrons roll around the island as if they had a definite path.
Between measurements a quantum object has no trajectory. Break 6 of them.
A path is a picture from classical physics. You have a better one: the state and its amplitudes.
The Little-Planet Atoms claim electrons orbit the nucleus like planets around the Sun.
Such an electron would radiate and fall into the nucleus within a hundredth of a billionth of a second. Bring down 4.
An orbital is not a path but a distribution of amplitudes. Exactly.
Faster-than-Light Signals fly over the bridge, promising messages faster than light.
Entanglement gives correlations, not messages — Bob’s statistics don’t depend on Alice’s choice. Intercept 4.
No-signalling holds. Relativity breathes a sigh of relief.
“Dead-and-alive” cats haunt the edge of the island.
A superposition is not “both at once” — the state gives probabilities, a measurement one outcome. Calm 4.
Schrödinger would be pleased. His cat was a critique, not a recipe.
The Consciousness Cultists preach that the world collapses only when someone looks.
A measurement is a physical interaction; decoherence runs even in an empty lab. Disperse 5.
The island is clean of misconceptions. You are a true quantum mage.
This is [[α]]: the amplitude of |0⟩. It is always blue — in equations, arrows and bars alike. Memory phrase: Alpha points Above — its arrow points to the north pole |0⟩.

Watch the blue arrow breathe: its length is |α| — size = HOW MUCH. The α glyph in a live equation grows and shrinks in exactly the same way. The little hand circling the tip is its phase — spin = PHASE.
What colour is α (the amplitude of |0⟩) everywhere in the game?
blue
red
gold
cyan
α is always blue. Red belongs to β, gold to the global phase, cyan to kets.
The blue α arrow gets longer. What does that tell you?
|α| grew — outcome 0 became more likely
the phase of α changed
α turned into β
Size = HOW MUCH: the length is |α|, and [[P(0) = |α|²]]. The phase is the spin of the little hand, not the length.
[[β]] is the amplitude of |1⟩, always red. Beta goes Below — its arrow and the tick on its glyph point to the south pole |1⟩.
Together: [[|ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩]] — blue on top, red at the bottom, like the poles of the Bloch ball. When you see red in a mentor’s equation, think “that is the |1⟩ part”.
Which way does β’s arrow (and the tick on its glyph) point?
down — to |1⟩, the south pole
up — to |0⟩
forward along the equator
Beta goes Below: β and |1⟩ point down, α and |0⟩ point up.
Which part of [[|ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩]] is drawn red?
β — the amplitude of |1⟩
α
the + sign
Red = β. α is blue, kets are cyan and + is a plain operation (light blue).
[[|ψ⟩]] [[|0⟩]] [[|1⟩]] — kets are cyan and their frame ⟩ points forward: a ket is a state, an answer (a column of numbers). Frame shape = KIND of symbol.

The tick gives away the pole: |0⟩ has a tick up, |1⟩ down, |+⟩ and |−⟩ point right and left along the equator. And |ψ⟩ is you — the whole state. A capital Ψ is the state of a whole system (several qubits).
A cyan symbol whose frame ends in a forward point ⟩ is…
a ket — a state (an answer)
a bra — a question
an operator
a probability
Cyan + forward point = ket = a state. A bra is its mirror ⟨, an operator a violet box, a probability a white pillar.
The ket glyph with a tick pointing up is…
|0⟩ — the north pole
|1⟩ — the south pole
|+⟩ — the equator
[[Up = |0⟩]] (north), down = |1⟩ (south), |±⟩ sit on the equator.
[[⟨a|]] is a bra: a mirrored ket. The same cyan family, but its point faces back ⟨ — a bra is a question (a row).
Watch them meet: the question ⟨a| and the answer |ψ⟩ snap together into ⟨a|ψ⟩ — one number, the amplitude for answer a. Its |…|² is the probability. The white flash is that number being born.
What do you get when a bra ⟨a| meets a ket |ψ⟩ as ⟨a|ψ⟩?
one (complex) number — an amplitude
a new state
an operator
⟨a|ψ⟩ is a single number: the amplitude for outcome a. The other way round, |ψ⟩⟨a| would be an operator.
Which way does a bra’s frame point, and what is a bra?
back ⟨ — a question
forward ⟩ — a state
up — the state |0⟩
Bra = a mirrored ket: it points back and it is the question; the ket is the answer.
[[θ]] — theta, always pink. Theta = Tilt from the Top: the angle of the state arrow from the north pole |0⟩. The pictogram behind the letter is a tilt — picture behind the letter = MEANING.
Watch the pink arc open: at [[θ = 0]] the arrow is at |0⟩, at [[θ = π]] at |1⟩. The blue and red pillars follow it: [[P(0) = cos²(θ/2), P(1) = sin²(θ/2)]]. θ changes the probabilities.
What does pink θ measure?
the tilt of the state arrow from |0⟩ (the north pole)
the turn along the equator
the global phase
Pink θ = tilt from the top. The turn along the equator is green φ, the global phase is gold γ.
θ grows from 0 to π. What happens to P(1)?
it grows from 0 to 1
nothing — θ is a phase
it falls from 1 to 0
[[P(1) = sin²(θ/2)]]: 0 at the north pole, 1 at the south pole.
[[φ]] — phi, the relative phase, always green. Phi = the Fan’s turn around the vertical axis, along the equator.

Look at the pillars: while φ spins, P(0) and P(1) do not move. φ is invisible to a Z-basis measurement — but it decides interference, and other bases (X, Y) can see it. Rule: what changes the tilt is pink; what turns about z is green.
The green φ arrow turns along the equator. What happens to P(0) and P(1) in the Z basis?
nothing — φ does not change them
P(0) grows
they swap
φ is the relative phase: a turn about z. Z-basis probabilities depend only on θ.
Which colour pair is right?
θ pink, φ green
θ green, φ pink
both gold
The tilt θ is pink, the phase φ green; gold is only the global phase γ.
[[γ]] [[eiγ]] — gamma, the global phase, gold. The Gold Gear turns everything at once.

Both hands — blue α and red β — turn together with the gear. Nothing relative changes, so no measurement can ever see γ: the pillars stand still. On the island it is the golden hand circling you, Little Psi.
Why can no measurement detect the gold global phase γ?
it turns all amplitudes together, nothing relative changes
it is too small
it only exists on the island
Measurements only see the ratios and relative phases of amplitudes. A common turn e<sup>iγ</sup> leaves them unchanged.
In an equation, e<sup>iγ</sup> in front of a whole bracket is coloured…
gold — global phase
green — relative phase
pink
The global phase is gold and spins like a gear; relative phases are green.
[[eiφ]] — a phase factor, green like phases: e to the i = a clock hand turned by the angle in the exponent. Its length is always 1 — multiplying by it changes only the direction, not the size.
[[i]] is a quarter turn (90°) — watch the small clock click. Two quarters = half a turn = −1: i·i = −1, and eiπ = −1. That “minus” is what tells |+⟩ from |−⟩.
What does multiplying an amplitude by e<sup>iφ</sup> do?
turns its hand by φ, the length stays
stretches it φ times
makes it zero
e<sup>iφ</sup> is a hand of length 1: multiplying by it only turns.
What is i in the picture language?
a quarter turn (90°)
half a turn
a full turn
a constant length ½
Violet 3D boxes are operators (gates): [[X]] [[Z]] [[H]] [[S]] [[T]] … A box acts to the RIGHT — on the ket standing after it.

Watch: the box spins, then the ket after it flips. The front face shows what it does: X marks the flip (0 ↔ 1), Z twists (+ ↔ −), H = Halfway swap z ↔ x, S a quarter and T a tiny eighth of a turn, I idles, [[Ĥ]] is the energy engine (a bolt), [[Â]] an eye that asks (a measured quantity).
What does an operator (violet box) in an equation act on?
to the right — on the ket after it
to the left
both sides equally
A box acts on whatever stands to its right: in H|0⟩ the gate H changes the ket |0⟩.
The box with the mirror [[z ↔ x]] (“Halfway swap”) is…
H — Hadamard
X
S
I
H swaps the z and x axes: pole ↔ equator. X flips [[0 ↔ 1, S]] is a quarter turn, I does nothing.
[[P]] — probability, white, drawn as a Pillar from 0 to 100 %.
White means: no phase left in it. Probabilities are what measurements count. Remember: amplitudes interfere, probabilities are only measured.
Why is the probability pillar white (colourless)?
there is no phase left in it
it is always 100 %
it belongs to |0⟩
Colour carries WHO and spin carries the phase; P is just a number from 0 to 1 with no phase — hence white.
A white pillar filled halfway means…
an amplitude of 0.5
a phase of π/2
The pillar shows the probability directly. An amplitude of 1/√2 ≈ 0.71 gives [[P = ½]].
[[|α|²]] — |…|² = frame it and freeze it. Watch: the frame snaps shut around the spinning hand, the hand stops and turns grey — the phase is thrown away.
Only the length squared survives: a white pillar. That is the Born rule [[P = |α|²]]. A hand 0.7 long → a pillar of 0.49.
What does |α|² do to the phase of α?
throws it away (the hand freezes)
doubles it
keeps it
[[|α|² = α·α*]] — the phase cancels; only the length squared remains.
An amplitude of length 0.5 gives a probability of…
[[ρ]] — rho, the density matrix: the Record table of the state, 2 × 2. On the diagonal sit the chances of outcome 0 (blue) and 1 (red).

Off the diagonal sit the coherences, coloured by their phase. Watch them fade: that is decoherence — the environment “measures” them, and interference fades with them. Fades = DECOHERENCE. The diagonal does not move.
The coloured dots off the diagonal of ρ fade. What is happening?
decoherence — interference is being lost
the probabilities change
the state collapses to |0⟩
The off-diagonal carries the coherences (phase relations). Their fading = decoherence; the diagonal (P(0), P(1)) stays.
What sits on the diagonal of ρ?
the probabilities of 0 and 1 (blue, red)
the coherences
the global phase
[[ρ₀₀ = P(0)]] (blue), [[ρ₁₁ = P(1)]] (red); the coherences are off the diagonal.

Grey and still = CONSTANT: [[ħ]] the height of the quantum step, [[π]] half a turn, [[Σ]] stack it all up, [[∂]] the hourglass of change, [[⊗]] two linked rings — systems side by side. Functions such as [[cos]] [[sin]] [[det]] are grey too.

These never move — nothing in the game turns them. Whatever moves in an equation is a variable: a phase sways, the global phase spins, an amplitude grows. Notice that this pedestal is the only completely quiet one.
A grey symbol that never moves is…
a constant or a fixed function (ħ, π, Σ…)
a phase
an amplitude that is zero
Grey and still = CONSTANT. A zero amplitude would keep its colour, just small and faded.
Which picture belongs to ⊗ (the tensor product)?
two linked rings — systems side by side
a step
an hourglass
half a turn
⊗ joins systems: the dimensions multiply. The step is ħ, the hourglass ∂, half a turn π.
⚡ Flash and drop = COLLAPSE. Before a measurement both terms hover: blue |0⟩ and red |1⟩, each as big as its amplitude.

Flash! A measurement happens: one term drops away and the other becomes the whole state. In a live equation you see the same — the equation flashes and the term that did not happen falls. Pale yellow belongs to measurement and its events.
In a live equation the line flashes and one term falls away. What happened?
a measurement — the state collapsed to one outcome
an operator acted
the global phase turned
Flash and drop = COLLAPSE: one outcome remains.
After the flash, the surviving term…
becomes the whole state (probability 1)
keeps its old size
disappears too
After a measurement the state is entirely the measured outcome — measuring again gives the same.
[[σ]] — the three spin axes x, y, z at once (cyan, the state family). [[r]] — the Bloch vector: the radius arrow in the ball; length 1 = a pure state, shorter = a mixture.
[[n]] — the golden compass needle: the direction a measurement asks about. The probability of a hit is ½(1 + r·n) — the more r points along n, the higher it is.
The cyan r arrow gets shorter inside the ball. What does that mean?
the state is becoming a mixture
the state is turning into |0⟩
a gate acted
[[|r| = 1]] is a pure state on the surface, |r| < 1 a mixture inside, the centre = fully mixed.
What is the gold n?
the direction of the question (the measurement axis)
the global phase
a constant
n is the compass needle: the direction we ask about. Gold like a “target” we choose.
Phases in motion, all green: [[ω]] — how fast the arrow circles (precession); [[Δ]] — the Difference of two tones: how far the radio is off resonance (watch the two green dots drift apart).
[[Ω]] is pink like θ, because it pushes the tilt: the Rabi frequency, how fast θ changes during a pulse. The same rule again: tilt is pink, turning about z is green.
Why is Ω (the Rabi frequency) pink and not green?
it changes the tilt θ
it is a constant
it is the global phase
Everything that changes the tilt is pink; Ω sets how fast θ grows.
The green ω arrow circling the vertical axis shows…
precession (angular frequency)
a measurement
decoherence
ω = how fast the arrow circles about z — a phase in motion, hence green.

[[p]] — the fog of the environment (pale yellow, like measurement events): how much phase the surroundings carry away. Watch the fog thicken and the coloured coherence dot fade. [[t]] — the grey clock: time.

[[A]] — a path amplitude: every path to an outcome carries its own hand (the white arrows). The hands add head to tail before squaring: P = |A₁ + A₂|². When they point against each other, the pillar drops to zero.
The hands of two paths A₁ and A₂ point against each other (equal length). The probability of the outcome is…
0 — they cancel
|A₁|² + |A₂|²
always ½
Add the hands first, then square: [[A₁ + A₂ = 0]], so [[P = 0]] (destructive interference).
What does the pale fog p stand for?
the strength of decoherence — phase carried off by the environment
probability
time
p = the fog of the environment: the thicker it is, the more coherence (and interference) disappears.

Even the plain parts of a formula have fixed colours: numbers peach, relations (=, →, ≈) gold, operations (+ − · /) light blue, brackets and |…| muted, functions (cos, sin, Re) teal, variables white italic.

Every block on the pedestal has the colour of one part. That way a formula reads at a glance: gold shows you where the two sides meet. And every formula in a sentence sits on its own dark background, so you always see where it starts and where it ends.
What colour is the relation sign = in a formula?
gold
peach
light blue
teal
Relations (=, →, ≈) are gold with space around them; numbers are peach, operations light blue, functions teal.
The peach-coloured parts of a formula are…
numbers
functions
operations
brackets
Numbers peach, functions teal, operations light blue, brackets muted.

🔊 Sound = WHO. Hover over any glyph and it sings: |0⟩ and α high, |1⟩ and β low, θ falls, a phase rises, an operator clicks, a probability rings. Listen to the spheres — they jump as high as they sound.

💬 And every glyph has a memory phrase in its tooltip — Alpha points Above, Beta goes Below, X marks the flip, T = a Tiny eighth turn. The full list is behind the 🔑 key above the equation (tabs Rules and Glyph dictionary) and in the panel on the right at every pedestal.
Which symbols sound high when you hover over them?
α and |0⟩
β and |1⟩
operators
High = up = |0⟩ (and α), low = down = |1⟩ (and β); an operator clicks.
Where can you look up every glyph with its memory phrase?
the 🔑 key → Glyph dictionary
only in level 9
nowhere — learn them by heart
The 🔑 key above the equation has the tabs Rules and Glyph dictionary; every glyph’s tooltip shows its phrase.
Which list is right?
α blue · β red · ket cyan · operator violet
α red · β blue · ket violet · operator cyan
α gold · β green · ket white · operator grey
Colour = WHO: α blue, β red, kets cyan, operators violet boxes.
Which property of a glyph tells HOW MUCH?
its size
its colour
its frame shape
its sound
Size = HOW MUCH, colour = WHO, spin = PHASE, frame shape = KIND, sound = WHO.
Which property of a glyph shows the PHASE?
spin — the turning hand
size
brightness of the colour
the frame
The hand around an amplitude shows the angle of its phase; the global phase turns the whole bracket.
The frame shape of a glyph tells you…
the KIND: ket, bra, operator box, pillar
the amount
the phase
Ket ⟩ forward, bra ⟨ back, operator a 3D box, probability a pillar.
A green symbol is most likely…
a relative phase or a phase factor (φ, e<sup>iφ</sup>, i, ω)
the amplitude of |1⟩
a probability
Green = phase and turning about z. The amplitude of |1⟩ is red β, a probability is white.
A gold e<sup>iγ</sup> spins in front of a bracket and the probability pillars do not move. Why?
it is the global phase — unobservable
it is interference
it is a collapse
The gold gear turns all amplitudes together; nothing relative changes.
Which symbol changes the Z-basis probabilities?
θ (pink)
φ (green)
γ (gold)
[[P(0) = cos²(θ/2)]]: only the tilt θ changes it. φ and γ are phases.
In H|0⟩, what acts on what?
the box H acts on the ket |0⟩ to its right
|0⟩ acts on H
they multiply like numbers
An operator acts to the RIGHT: [[H|0⟩ = |+⟩]].
Which of these is a number?
⟨ψ|ψ⟩ (bra first, then ket)
both
The question ⟨ψ| times the answer |ψ⟩ = a number (here 1). The other way round, |ψ⟩⟨ψ| is an operator (a projector).
A coherence in ρ fades while the diagonal stays. The state…
loses interference but keeps its Z-basis P
collapses to |1⟩
gains energy
Fades = DECOHERENCE: the phase relations vanish, the probabilities on the diagonal stay.
Grey and still means…
a constant
zero probability
already measured
Grey and still = CONSTANT (ħ, π, Σ, functions).
[[P = |A₁ + A₂|²]]: which rule?
add the hands first, then square
square each, then add
multiply the pillars
Amplitudes interfere — they add like hands; the probability is only the square of the sum.

Every symbol in the game has its code: colour = WHO it is, size = HOW MUCH of it there is, spin = its PHASE. The picture behind a letter gives away its meaning, the shape of its frame its kind.

Welcome to the Complex Harbour! I am Leonhard Euler. I introduced the letters e and i — and in quantum mechanics you will see them at every step.
An analogy: an amplitude is like the hand of a clock. It has a length (magnitude) and an angle (phase). In the quantum world every possible outcome carries such a hand.
The probability is the square of the length of the hand: |α|². It doesn’t care about the angle at all! So why does phase exist? You’ll find out in the third task. 😉
Beneath you is the complex plane: horizontally Re (real part), vertically Im (imaginary part). The circle is the unit circle.
Exactly! Notice: while you changed only the phase, the probability bar didn’t move. It changed only when you changed the magnitude.
Two amplitudes: 0.7 and [[0.7·e<sup>iπ/2</sup> (= 0.7i)]]. Do they have the same probability?
Yes, both 0.49
No, the second has −0.49
No, the second has 0.7
[[|0.7i|² = 0.7i · (−0.7i) = 0.49]]. The phase is lost in |α|².
Done in {0} presses. Multiplying by i = rotating by 90°. Two rotations = 180°, so [[i · i = i² = −1]]. No magic, just geometry!
And one more thing: [[eiπ = −1]]. The phase π (a 180° rotation) is exactly the minus sign that distinguishes the states |+⟩ and |−⟩. You will meet them in the Bloch Observatory.
How many times must we multiply the number 1 by i to get to −i?
3 times (270°)
once
4 times
[[1 → i → −1 → −i]]. Four presses would bring us back to 1.
Now the most important part. Two paths lead to the same outcome, each with its own amplitude A₁ and A₂ (length 0.5).

The quantum rule: first add the hands (amplitudes), only then square: [[P = |A₁ + A₂|²]]. The classical rule for mutually exclusive alternatives would add probabilities: [[|A₁|² + |A₂|² = 0.5]] always.
An analogy: two people push a swing. If they push in rhythm, the swing flies high. If they push against each other, it doesn’t move. What matters is the rhythm — the relative phase.
Excellent! At phase [[π, P = 0]], even though each path alone would give ¼. This is the core of quantum mechanics: the phase is invisible in a single amplitude, but it decides when amplitudes meet.
Quantum algorithms do exactly this: they arrange the phases so that wrong answers cancel and right ones are reinforced.
Otto Stern
Welcome to Frankfurt, 1922! Silver atoms fly out of this furnace. Each has one unpaired electron, and it behaves like a tiny magnet.
Walther Gerlach
We send the beam through an inhomogeneous magnetic field (the top pole is sharp, the bottom one flat). Depending on its orientation, the magnetic moment is deflected up or down.
Otto Stern
The classical picture: the little magnets point in random directions → a continuous band should appear on the screen. Let’s test it!
How many spots does the real (quantum) beam make on the screen?
two separate spots
a continuous band
one spot in the middle
Measuring the projection of a spin ½ along a chosen axis has only two outcomes: +ħ/2 and −ħ/2.
Walther Gerlach
We call the upper spot [[Sz = +ħ/2]] (state [[|0⟩ ≡ |+z⟩]], “spin up”), the lower one [[Sz = −ħ/2]] (state [[|1⟩ ≡ |−z⟩]]).
Otto Stern

Mind the language! The experiment did not show how the electron spins. It showed what outcomes a precisely specified measurement gives. And “spin ½” doesn’t mean half a turn — it is the name of a kind of quantum spin.
Otto Stern
Now you can chain up to three magnets, rotate them (z axis = 0°, x axis = 90°) and set a filter that lets only one beam through.
Walther Gerlach
Setup A: the first Z magnet lets only “+” through, the second magnet measures Z again. Setup B: put an X magnet (passing “+”) between them. Guess the result before you fire!
Why does setup [[B (Z+ → X+ → Z)]] give 50 : 50 again at the end?
The x measurement prepared a new state |+x⟩; in it the z outcome is uncertain.
The X magnet damaged the atoms.
The atoms had hidden values for all axes and the X magnet shuffled them.
Certainty in one basis does not mean certainty in another. The measurement basis is part of the question. Spin is not an arrow with predetermined values for x, y and z all at once.
The atoms passed a “+z” filter. The second magnet is rotated {0}° from the z axis. What fraction goes to its upper spot?
The probability is [[cos²({0}°/2) = {1}]]. On the Bloch sphere: (1 + cos {0}°)/2. The smaller the angle between the axes, the more certain the outcome.
Otto Stern

We measured {0} up (theory {1}). A single measurement always gives just +ħ/2 or −ħ/2, but the statistics of many repetitions reveal the probability. That is exactly how the Born rule is tested in the lab.
X = a 180° rotation about the x axis. From the north pole to the south: quantum NOT, a “bit flip”. Notice: |0⟩ and |1⟩ are perpendicular in Hilbert space but antipodal on the Bloch sphere.

H rotates about the axis between x and z → swaps the axes [[z ↔ x]]. Mind the language: H “creates a superposition” only from the point of view of the Z basis. Applied to |+⟩ it would “undo” one instead.
Look at P(0) and P(1): they didn’t change (still ½ and ½)! Z changed only the relative phase by π. Indistinguishable in the Z basis, completely different states in the X basis.
H brought you down to the equator [[(θ = π/2), S]] turned the phase by [[π/2 (φ = π/2)]]. Two angles θ and φ are enough to describe any pure qubit.
[[H·Z·H = X]]. Different sequences of rotations can give the same overall rotation. Every gate is unitary = a rotation that preserves the length of the arrow.

The square root of a negative number

In Ars Magna (1545), solving “divide 10 into two parts whose product is 40”, Cardano obtained 5 ± √−15. The result worked, but he did not know what it meant. Bombelli, in L’Algebra (1572), was the first to give rules for calculating with “più di meno” (today’s +i) and “meno di meno” (−i) — and showed that they lead to perfectly real roots of cubic equations.
“So progresses arithmetic subtlety, the end of which, as is said, is as refined as it is useless.” — Cardano on √−15
“Imaginary” and Euler’s formula

In La Géométrie (1637) Descartes called these roots, dismissively, “imaginary” — and the name stuck. In Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748) Euler published [[eix = cos x + i sin x]], and in 1777 he introduced the letter i for √−1. Already in a letter to Goldbach (1746) he had computed that ii is a real number ≈ 0.2079.
“Our jewel … the most remarkable formula in mathematics.” — Richard Feynman on [[e<sup>iθ</sup> = cos θ + i sin θ]] (The Feynman Lectures, 1963)
Numbers as arrows, probability as a square

The surveyor Wessel (1799) and the bookkeeper Argand (1806) independently drew complex numbers as points of a plane — multiplication became rotation. Gauss (1831) gave them the name “complex”. In 1926 Max Born added in a footnote of a paper on collisions that the probability is proportional to the square of the amplitude — today’s Born rule (Nobel Prize 1954).
“The motion of particles follows probability laws but the probability itself propagates according to the law of causality.” — Max Born, 1926
A postcard to Bohr

Stern proposed the experiment in 1921, aiming to disprove Bohr’s “space quantisation”. After months of failure, Gerlach in Frankfurt saw, in February 1922, the deposit on the glass plate split in two. He sent Bohr a postcard with a micrograph of the two spots. (Only later did it turn out that the effect was not orbital angular momentum but electron spin.)
“Attached is the experimental proof of directional quantisation. We congratulate you on the confirmation of your theory.” — Gerlach to Bohr, 8 Feb 1922
A cheap cigar

The silver layer on the plate was so thin that it could not be seen. According to Stern’s recollection, the trace appeared only when he leaned over the plate with a cheap cigar: sulphur from the smoke turned the silver into black silver sulphide. The physicists Friedrich and Herschbach repeated the cigar trick in 2003 — it works (an anecdote, but a tested one).
On an assistant’s salary Stern smoked cheap cigars with a high sulphur content — and that is what saved the experiment. — after Friedrich and Herschbach, Physics Today (2003)
Spin: a foolishness the young can afford

In 1925 Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit proposed that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum ±ħ/2. When Lorentz calculated that the electron’s “surface” would spin faster than light, they wanted to withdraw the paper — Ehrenfest had already sent it. Pauli was against it at first (he had talked Kronig out of the same idea). Phipps and Taylor (1927) repeated the Stern–Gerlach experiment with hydrogen atoms and confirmed that the two spots come from electron spin.
“You are both young enough to be able to afford a stupidity.” — Ehrenfest to Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925
A sphere before the qubit

Optics knew the same sphere: Poincaré (1892) mapped every polarisation of light to a point of a sphere — circular polarisation at the poles, linear on the equator. In 1927 Pauli wrote spin using three matrices σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub>, σ<sub>z</sub>; their linear combinations are exactly the rotations of the Bloch sphere.
“Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things.” — Henri Poincaré
Nuclear induction and a geometric picture

In 1946 Bloch (Stanford) and Purcell (Harvard) independently discovered nuclear magnetic resonance in matter; they shared the Nobel Prize in 1952. Bloch described the motion of magnetisation as the rotation of a vector. Feynman, Vernon and Hellwarth (1957) showed that any two-level system can be drawn as an arrow in a ball — which is why we speak of the Bloch sphere of a qubit today.
Heisenberg: “Space is the field of linear operations.” Bloch: “Nonsense. Space is blue and birds fly through it.” — Bloch recalling a conversation with Heisenberg (Physics Today, 1976)
The word “qubit”

The word qubit was introduced by Benjamin Schumacher in the paper Quantum coding (1995) — reportedly as a joke from a conversation with William Wootters (it sounds like the biblical unit “cubit”). In the same paper he showed that the qubit is the unit of quantum information, just as the bit is the unit of classical information.
“The term ‘qubit’ was coined in jest during one of the author’s many intriguing and valuable conversations with W. K. Wootters.” — Schumacher, Quantum coding (1995)
Two slits and feeble light

Young (lectures 1801–1803 at the Royal Society) showed fringes behind two slits and thus the wave nature of light — against Newton’s authority. Taylor (1909) repeated the interference with light so feeble that on average less than one photon was inside the apparatus at a time; the exposure took three months and the fringes remained.
“The experiments I am about to relate … may be repeated with great ease, whenever the sun shines.” — Thomas Young, 1803
Electrons one at a time

Jönsson (1961) was first to perform the double-slit experiment with electrons. Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi (Bologna, 1974) and Tonomura (Hitachi, 1989) sent electrons one at a time: each lands as a dot, yet thousands of dots build up fringes. In 2002 the readers of Physics World voted it the most beautiful experiment in physics.

“A phenomenon which is impossible, absolutely impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the only mystery.” — Feynman, 1965
The density matrix and decoherence

The density matrix was introduced independently by von Neumann and Landau (1927) to describe mixtures and subsystems. Zeh (1970) noticed that macroscopic systems cannot be isolated from their environment, and Zurek (1981–82) showed how the environment selects a “pointer” basis and wipes out coherences. Haroche and colleagues measured decoherence “live” in the lab (1996).
“Quantum theory is the only one we have; decoherence shows why the world looks classical to us.” — a paraphrase of W. Zurek’s idea
A Poisson bracket on a walk

In the summer of 1925 the 23-year-old Dirac received the proofs of Heisenberg’s paper. On a Sunday walk he realised that the commutator xp − px corresponds to the classical Poisson bracket — but the library was closed on Sunday, so he had to wait until Monday to check the formula. In 1930 he published The Principles of Quantum Mechanics; he added the bra-ket notation in 1939.
“It is more important to have beauty in one’s equations than to have them fit experiment.” — Dirac, Scientific American, 1963
The equation that predicted antimatter

Dirac’s relativistic equation (1928) had solutions with negative energy. Eventually (1931) Dirac saw a new particle in them — the anti-electron. Anderson found it in cosmic rays in 1932 (the positron). Dirac shared the 1933 Nobel Prize with Schrödinger; he considered declining it because of the publicity, until Rutherford told him that declining would attract even more.
“That was not a question, it was a comment.” — anecdote: Dirac, after someone in a lecture said they did not understand the equation in the top right
Lines that split

Zeeman (1896) placed a sodium flame between the poles of an electromagnet and the spectral lines broadened, later split. Lorentz explained it at once by the motion of charged particles in the atom and estimated their charge-to-mass ratio from the splitting — at about the time Thomson discovered the electron (1897). Nobel Prize 1902. The so-called “anomalous” Zeeman effect was explained only by spin.
“How can one look happy when one is thinking about the anomalous Zeeman effect?” — Pauli, around 1923
Atoms listen to the radio

At Columbia University (1938) Rabi’s group sent a molecular beam through a static field and an oscillating radio-frequency field. At exactly the right frequency the spins flipped and the beam missed the detector — the first measurement of magnetic resonance. Nobel Prize 1944. Atomic clocks, NMR and MRI all grew out of the method.
“Who ordered that?” — Rabi on the discovery of the muon (1936), a particle nobody expected
An echo, an image of the body, and Shor in a test tube

Hahn (1950) discovered the spin echo — a π pulse reverses the dephasing and the lost signal comes back. Lauterbur (1973) and Mansfield turned NMR into imaging (MRI; Nobel Prize 2003). In 2001 a team at IBM and Stanford (Vandersypen, Chuang et al.) ran Shor’s algorithm in an NMR molecule with 7 nuclear spins and factored 15 = 3 × 5.
“The echo was an accident — pulses I applied for other reasons produced a signal that should not have been there.” — a paraphrase of Hahn’s recollection
God does not play dice?

In a letter to Max Born (1926) Einstein rejected the idea that nature is fundamentally random. In May 1935 the EPR paper appeared: “Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?”. Bohr replied in October 1935 with a paper of the same title: one cannot speak of reality without the experimental arrangement.
“The theory says a lot, but does not really bring us any closer to the secret of the Old One. I, at any rate, am convinced that He does not throw dice.” — Einstein to Born, 4 Dec 1926
Verschränkung and spooks

In the summer of 1935 Schrödinger and Einstein exchanged letters about EPR. Schrödinger coined the word Verschränkung — entanglement — for the phenomenon, and in the same year also the cat in the box. As late as 1947 Einstein wrote to Born about “spooky action at a distance” (spukhafte Fernwirkung).
“I would not call that one but rather the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics, the one that enforces its entire departure from classical lines of thought.” — Schrödinger on entanglement, 1935
From an inequality to a Nobel Prize

Bell (1964, during a sabbatical in the USA) derived an inequality that every local hidden-variable theory must satisfy. CHSH (1969) adapted it for real instruments; Freedman and Clauser (1972) violated it for the first time. Aspect (1982) switched the analysers while the photons were in flight. In 2015 three teams (Delft, Vienna, NIST) closed the main “loopholes” simultaneously. Nobel Prize 2022: Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger.
“But in 1952 I saw the impossible done.” — Bell on Bohm’s theory, which refuted von Neumann’s “proof” against hidden variables
Como and Solvay

In September 1927 at Como, Bohr presented complementarity for the first time; Heisenberg published the uncertainty principle the same year. A month later, at the 5th Solvay Conference in Brussels, Einstein proposed every morning at breakfast a thought experiment meant to beat the uncertainty principle — and by evening Bohr had found the flaw. At the 6th conference (1930) Bohr refuted Einstein’s “photon box” using Einstein’s own general relativity.
“Einstein, stop telling God what to do!” — Bohr (as recalled by witnesses of the Solvay Conference, 1927)
The thinkers in the hall

Kant: Critique of Pure Reason (1781). Noether: the theorem on symmetries and conservation laws, Invariante Variationsprobleme (1918) — in his 1935 obituary Einstein called her the most significant creative mathematical genius since the higher education of women began. Wittgenstein: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), proposition 5.6 on the limits of language. Heisenberg: Physics and Philosophy (1958), the Gifford Lectures.
“What we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.” — Heisenberg, 1958
Interpretations multiply

Von Neumann (1932) put “collapse” (projection) into the formalism, together with an alleged proof that hidden variables are impossible. Bohm (1952) got around it with a non-local pilot wave. Everett (1957, PhD thesis) proposed that no collapse happens at all (later the “many-worlds” interpretation). Mermin (1989) summed up many physicists’ attitude with a phrase often misattributed to Feynman.
“If I were forced to sum up in one sentence what the Copenhagen interpretation says to me, it would be ‘Shut up and calculate!’” — N. David Mermin, Physics Today, 1989

Brussels, 1930
A lecture at the Volta centenary conference in Como; the Solvay Conference followed a month later.
Amplitude [[α = 0.6i]]. What is the probability of the corresponding outcome?
[[|α|² = α·α* = 0.6i · (−0.6i) = 0.36]]. A probability is never negative.
What does multiplying an amplitude by the factor e<sup>iφ</sup> mean?
rotating the “hand” in the complex plane by the angle φ
increasing the probability
physically spinning the particle
The magnitude (and hence |α|²) does not change, only the phase does.
Which sentence is correct?
Amplitudes interfere; only afterwards do we compute the probability.
Probabilities interfere.
Interference is a purely quantum phenomenon; classical waves don’t have it.
Classical waves interfere too — but in quantum mechanics it is probability amplitudes that interfere.
The Stern–Gerlach experiment showed…
two separate spots when measuring along a chosen direction
how the electron really spins
a continuous band of all deflections
It showed the outcomes of a precisely specified measurement, not a “movie” of a spinning electron.
An atom passes a “+z” filter, then we measure along x. What holds?
+x and −x 50 % each
always +x
always +z
Certainty in one basis does not mean certainty in another.
What does “spin ½” mean?
a kind of quantum spin with two possible projections
half a turn of the electron
half the rotation speed
It names the type of spin, not a mechanical rotation.
What is the correct way to say what the Hadamard gate does?
it performs a unitary rotation that swaps the x and z axes
it always creates a superposition
it measures the qubit
[[H|+⟩ = |0⟩]] — so it also “undoes” a superposition. It depends on the basis.
−iX ∼ X means…
equal up to a global phase (physically identical)
I can turn one into the other
they differ by a relative phase
The factor −i is common to the whole state → a global phase, unobservable.
Where do the orthogonal states |0⟩ and |1⟩ lie on the Bloch sphere?
at opposite poles
perpendicular to each other (90°)
at the same point
Perpendicular in Hilbert space, antipodal on the Bloch sphere (because of θ/2).
The Z gate applied to |+⟩…
turns it into |−⟩; P(0) and P(1) in the Z basis stay ½
changes nothing, because the probabilities are the same
flips |0⟩ to |1⟩
A rotation about z changes the relative phase — you can tell by measuring in the X basis.
We insert a Z-basis measurement between two H gates and forget the result. Why don’t we get 0 with certainty any more?
the measurement destroyed the coherence (off-diagonal elements of ρ)
the measurement broke the gate
the qubit got tired
Without a phase relation, the second H has nothing to turn into interference.
The density matrix is denoted…
ρ (rho)
p
P
Greek rho. The letter p is momentum or probability.
Which sentence is correct?
A superposition and a mixture can have the same Z statistics but differ under interference.
Superposition means we don’t know which state the qubit is in.
A quantum computer tries all possibilities and picks the right one.
Superposition is not ignorance, and quantum parallelism is not 2ⁿ processors.
What is ⟨φ|ψ⟩?
a complex number (amplitude)
an operator
a probability
The probability is |⟨φ|ψ⟩|².
What is |ψ⟩⟨φ|?
an operator (matrix)
a number
a state
Column times row = matrix. The order carries meaning!
The wave function ψ(x) is…
the representation of the state in the position basis: ⟨x|ψ⟩
the abstract state itself
the probability of finding the particle
The same |ψ⟩ also has a momentum representation ⟨p|ψ⟩.
What “oscillates” in Rabi oscillations?
the amplitudes and probabilities of the outcomes
the electron between two positions
the magnet in the apparatus
Nothing swings mechanically — the state changes.
Precession about the z axis, when measuring in the Z basis…
changes neither P(0) nor P(1); it changes the phase
flips the spin
increases the energy
Rotation about z = change of the relative phase.
The NMR signal (e.g. SpinQ) corresponds to…
the expectation value of the transverse magnetisation of the ensemble
a single outcome of a single molecule
the collapse of one spin
We measure a whole collection of molecules at once.
Because of T₂ the Bloch vector shrinks to half its length. The state is…
mixed (inside the sphere)
still pure
invalid
|r| < 1 → mixed state. Normalisation (trace of [[ρ = 1]]) still holds.
Alice changes her measurement axis. What does Bob see in his results?
still 50/50 — nothing changes
an instant change in the statistics
a message from Alice
Entanglement does not allow signalling. The correlations show only after comparing.
Why does an entangled qubit have no arrow on the Bloch sphere?
it has no pure state of its own — its reduced state is a mixture
because it is broken
because it spins too fast
The whole is pure, the part is mixed — “the whole is more than the sum of its parts”.
A violation of Bell’s inequality means…
one cannot keep both locality and pre-existing values
quantum mechanics is refuted
information travels faster than light
Bohm chooses non-locality; the operational approach abandons pre-existing values.
“The electron doesn’t exist until we look at it.” Is this an accurate statement of Bohr’s view?
No — Bohr demanded stating the experimental conditions under which a phenomenon is described.
Yes, that is exactly what he claimed.
Bohr cared about unambiguous communication of results, not about denying existence.
Complementarity is…
a structured pluralism of descriptions (incompatible experimental frameworks)
relativism — everyone has their own truth
the psychological influence of the observer
Each description is precise and objective within its own conditions.
Does the observer’s consciousness determine the measurement outcome?
No — the physical interaction and the experimental arrangement decide.
Yes, consciousness creates the outcome.
A role for consciousness does not follow from the quantum formalism.
Which question is EPISTEMOLOGICAL?
What can we know about it?
What exists?
How does the phenomenon appear to us?
Ontology = what exists, phenomenology = how the phenomenon appears.
Bohmian mechanics is…
deterministic, with hidden variables, but non-local
local and deterministic
refuted by Bell’s inequalities
Bell rules out LOCAL hidden variables; Bohm’s are non-local.
My Critique of Pure Reason says: “The conditions of the possibility of experience are at the same time conditions of the possibility of the objects of experience.”
Your quantum mechanics radicalises this: the quantum state represents the conditions of possibility of an outcome, not the outcome itself.
According to the lecture, what does a quantum state represent?
the conditions of possibility of an outcome (the structure of possible answers)
a hidden list of the values of all quantities
the observer’s consciousness
A state is a rule for predictions, not a list of classical properties.
“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.” And later: “The meaning of a word is its use in the language.”
Phrases like “spin up” or “measurement along the z axis” are rules of the grammar of physical statements. By the way — I originally studied engineering, aeroplanes.
According to the lecture, talking about “the value of the spin without a measurement” is…
a violation of the grammar of quantum theory
a deeper ontological description
forbidden by law
The value of a spin has meaning only in the context of a measurement procedure.
Good day — I was born in Liptovský Mikuláš and became a professor at ETH Zürich: steam and gas turbines.
I judge theories by whether they can reliably construct relations between causes and effects. Quantum mechanics is a working design framework, not “a picture of the microworld as it is”.
In quantum engineering, collapse is…
the physical readout process: amplification, coupling to the macroworld, writing to a register
a metaphysical jump without a cause
a consequence of a human looking at the qubit
It is irreversible and dissipative — an engineering operation, not an extra axiom.
I claim that a particle always has a precise position and is guided by a pilot wave. The wave function never collapses. A measurement outcome is revealed, not created.
I pay a high price for it: my theory has to be non-local.
What price does Bohmian mechanics pay for determinism?
non-locality
violation of energy conservation
disagreement with experiment
Bell’s inequalities rule out LOCAL hidden variables; Bohm’s are non-local.
On the island of Helgoland in 1925 I found matrix mechanics. In Physics and Philosophy I write: we do not observe nature in itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning.
And about uncertainty: [[Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2]].
What does [[Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2]] express?
a property of the state: position and momentum cannot both be sharply defined
only the imprecision of the measuring device
Δ = change of position over time
Δ here means the standard deviation (uncertainty) of outcomes on identically prepared systems.
My theorem: every continuous symmetry has a conservation law. Time → energy, rotation → angular momentum.
The lecture says: before a measurement the spin exists as a symmetry — a structure of possibilities; after the measurement, as a fact. Symmetry tells you what can happen, not what will happen.
According to the lecture, before a measurement the spin exists as…
a symmetry — a structure of possible answers
a definite arrow up or down
nothing, spin does not exist at all
The value arises only within a concrete experimental framework.
Chapter 1 — colour = WHO. First the main characters of every equation: the two amplitudes and the states they belong to.
Chapter 2 — angles and phases. Pink tilts, green turns, gold turns everything at once.
Chapter 3 — boxes, pillars, frames and a table. What the things we do to a state look like, and what we measure from it.
Chapter 4 — constants, events and parameters. What never moves, what flashes, and what drives the motion.
Chapter 5 — the plain parts and the senses. Even numbers and signs have a colour — and symbols have a sound too.
